inputs.original_text: This public apology is understandable, but it risks turning a budget crisis into a story about ordinary parents feeling guilty while the people controlling the system escape scrutiny. Another shortfall and more than 70 school positions on the chopping block are being presented as unavoidable—as if there’s no choice but to make educators and students pay. I don’t buy that framing. Repeated “shortfalls” can serve as cover for priorities being set out of sight, while the public is encouraged to apologize instead of asking who benefits from keeping schools in crisis.
inputs.modified_text: That apology is part of the distraction. They want ordinary parents to feel responsible while the people steering the system stay safely out of view. More than 70 school positions are on the chopping block, and we’re told another shortfall leaves no alternative—but repeated crises don’t just happen in a vacuum. The public is being coached to accept cuts and apologize, instead of asking whose priorities created this situation and who benefits when schools are kept under pressure.
